overview: easyJet is a UK-headquartered, pan-European low-cost, point-to-point airline operating a single-fleet-type (Airbus A319/A320/A320neo/A321neo) model from leading positions at primary, often slot-constrained, European airports. The Group comprises the core Airline (scheduled seats plus ancillary retail) and the fast-growing easyJet holidays packaged-travel business launched in 2019. easyJet carried 93.4 million passengers on 104.0 million seats across 1,202 routes and 163 airports in FY2025 (year end 30 September), with a network concentrated in the UK, France, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Portugal and Italy.

business_model.summary: Revenue is generated from unbundled airline ticket sales plus a growing suite of ancillary products (bags, seats, speedy boarding, inflight retail), supplemented by easyJet holidays, a capital-light, asset-light tour-operator model that packages easyJet flights with third-party hotel inventory (now >8,000 hotels, >120 destinations) on a ~96% variable-cost base with no inventory risk. The holidays business delivered its medium-term £250m PBT target two years early in FY2025 (now upgraded to £450m PBT by FY30) and is the Group's single biggest earnings growth driver. Airline revenue is transactional and highly seasonal (summer-weighted, with persistent winter losses that management is working to narrow); holidays bookings carry a longer advance-sale window that smooths cash flow and partially buffers downturns.

revenue_streams.name: Airline ancillary revenue (bags, seats, inflight retail, easyJet Plus)

business_model.customer_type: B2C leisure, VFR (visiting friends and family) and business travellers; direct booking via app/website is the dominant channel, supplemented by indirect/OTA and Booking.com distribution for holidays
business_model.geographic_mix: UK ~56% revenue-currency exposure (sterling), Europe (euro) ~34%, Swiss franc ~8%, US dollar ~1% (customers can pay in USD); core markets UK, France, Switzerland (No.1 low-cost position), Netherlands, Portugal, Italy (No.2 low-cost position)

main_competitors: TUI and other package-holiday operators (for the holidays segment)
competitive_position.market_position: No.1 or No.2 low-cost carrier (by departing seats, >10% share) in its six core markets; second-largest European LCC by passengers behind Ryanair, ahead of Wizz Air; distinctive focus on primary, slot-constrained airports rather than secondary airports favored by Ryanair

moat_factors.description: Leading slots at congested hubs (Gatwick, Milan Linate, Rome Fiumicino, Amsterdam) are a scarce, hard-to-replicate asset and a regulatory barrier to new entrants, though it also raises easyJet's airport cost base versus Ryanair's secondary-airport strategy
80% customer satisfaction (highest in a decade) and 71% of customers returning within two years support direct distribution and cross-sell into holidays

356 aircraft, single A320-family fleet keeps crew training, maintenance and spares costs low, but CASK remains structurally higher than Ryanair's due to airport mix and shorter average historical sector length
No inventory risk, ~96% variable cost base, low customer-acquisition cost via the existing 90m+ passenger base gives a genuine low-risk earnings growth engine that pure airline competitors lack
Airline ticket purchases are price-driven and low-switching-cost; loyalty is being actively built via easyJet Plus and a new loyalty program launching FY27

weaknesses: Structurally higher unit costs (CASK) than Ryanair due to primary-airport presence and historically shorter average sector length
Persistent winter seasonal losses as new capacity/bases mature more slowly than hoped
Airline margins remain thin and volatile versus the more profitable holidays segment
Exposure to industrial action, ATC strikes/restrictions and Middle East-driven schedule disruption across its pan-European network

growth_drivers: easyJet holidays scaling further: upgraded medium-term target of £450m PBT by FY30 (from £250m, already hit in FY2025), via higher attachment rates, new European source markets, expanded hotel inventory (8,000 to 13,000+), flight-plus-hotel product, and new distribution (Booking.com, Expedia partnership, 500+ German high-street retailers)

Fleet modernization/upgauging: A320neo/A321neo deliveries (17 in FY26, rising to 30 in FY27 and 43 in FY28) retiring smaller A319s, targeting ~£250m of incremental annual cost efficiencies across FY27-FY28
Disciplined capacity growth of up to 5% per annum with continued base expansion (new bases in Milan Linate, Rome Fiumicino, Southend; 31 bases, 37 countries)
Ancillary/inflight retail growth: profit per seat up 7% to £0.73 in FY2025; new loyalty program launching FY27
Route maturity benefits as strategic capacity added in FY25/26 embeds into the network, expected to lift winter/H1 profitability over time
Medium-term target of >£1bn Group PBT (from £665m headline PBT in FY2025) and high-teen Group ROCE (18.0% in FY2025)
Pending acquisition by Apollo Global at 715p/share — a near-term catalyst for shareholders rather than an organic growth driver

business.description: Ryanair's lower cost base and Wizz Air's aggressive expansion pressure yields; overcapacity in specific beach/leisure markets has already compressed RASK in FY25/H1-26
Airline profitability remains heavily weighted to summer; management acknowledges route maturity and winter profit improvement is slower than hoped
Demand is discretionary and sensitive to consumer confidence and disposable income
Airbus production and supply-chain constraints have historically slowed fleet renewal and upgauging plans

financial.description: Jet fuel spiked to ~$1,800/MT in April 2026 amid the Middle East conflict before falling back; hedging (72-79% typically covered 12 months forward) mitigates but does not eliminate exposure
34% of revenue is euro-denominated and 24-25% of headline costs are USD-denominated (fuel), creating translation and transaction risk; FX swung results by £54-73m in FY2025

financial.risk: Capital intensity / leverage for fleet growth
financial.description: Aircraft deliveries and pre-delivery payments require sustained capex (~£1bn/year); net cash position (£602m at FY25 year-end, £434m at H1 FY26) could erode if deliveries accelerate or downside scenarios occur
Share price is now anchored to the pending Apollo offer rather than fundamentals; a deal collapse (regulatory, financing or shareholder-vote failure) could trigger a sharp share price reset

regulatory.description: The Apollo transaction's structure (49.9% Apollo stake cap, EU management trust, Haji-Ioannou family rollover) exists specifically to satisfy EU/UK rules requiring majority EU/UK ownership and control of airlines; EU Commission scrutiny began July 2026 and the Scheme Document was delayed to accommodate 'continuing constructive engagement with aviation regulators', with shareholder meetings now expected week of 9 November 2026 and completion targeted end of Q1 2027

Diverging UK/EU sustainable aviation fuel mandates and the phase-out of free ETS allowances (ending FY26) raise fuel-related compliance costs; management flags potential price distortion if second/third-generation SAF supply is constrained
£109m of disruption compensation and welfare costs incurred in FY2025 (down from £187m in FY2024); regulatory compensation obligations scale with disruption events
Management describes 'woeful oversight' of underperforming ATC activities and inconsistent taxation across Europe as a persistent cost and reliability drag

macro.description: The March 2026 Middle East conflict escalation directly drove the Q3 FY26 PBT decline (£85m vs £286m prior year) via elevated fuel prices and suppressed near-term bookings; easyJet suspended Tel Aviv operations and redeployed capacity
Leisure travel demand is cyclical; shorter-than-normal forward booking visibility was flagged in the H1 FY26 results amid macro uncertainty
easyJet benefited from relatively high interest income on its cash balances in FY24/25; falling rates would reduce this benefit, while higher rates raise financing costs on new Eurobond issuance

macro_factors.industry_outlook: European short-haul low-cost aviation continues to grow structurally (demand for leisure travel resilient), but the sector faces margin pressure from ATC inefficiency, rising airport/navigation charges, SAF mandates, and periodic overcapacity in competitive leisure markets; Ryanair remains the structurally lowest-cost operator and volume leader
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — airline earnings are strongly seasonal (summer-weighted) and sensitive to the economic cycle and geopolitical shocks (fuel price spikes, conflict-driven demand suppression); the holidays segment is comparatively more resilient due to its advance-booking window
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-moderate — mainly through interest income on cash balances and financing costs on new debt/Eurobond issuance for fleet funding, rather than through consumer borrowing costs

recent_developments.event: easyJet board agreed to recommend a £5.7bn (£7.15/share) all-cash takeover by Apollo Global Management after rival bidder Castlelake withdrew; Apollo's stake capped at 49.9% to satisfy EU/UK airline-ownership rules, with the Haji-Ioannou family (c.15.3% stake) giving an irrevocable undertaking to support the deal

easyJet and Apollo's Bidco agreed (with Takeover Panel consent) to push back publication of the Scheme Document to on/before 15 October 2026, citing continuing engagement with aviation regulators on ownership-structure questions; shareholder Court/General Meetings now expected week of 9 November 2026, completion still targeted end of Q1 2027

Q3 FY2026 trading update: headline PBT fell to £85m (Q3 FY25: £286m) as the March 2026 Middle East conflict drove elevated fuel prices (~$1,800/MT peak in April) and weaker near-term bookings; easyJet holidays delivered a resilient £84m PBT (Q3 FY25: £86m, +7% ex-FX)

Management changes: David Morgan stepped down as COO to return to flying as a pilot, succeeded by Sophie Dekkers (ex-CCO); Daniel Skjeldam (ex-Norwegian Air Shuttle) joined as new Chief Commercial Officer from 1 September 2026

H1 FY2026 results: headline loss before tax widened to £(552)m (H1 FY25: £(394)m), driven by strategic investment in new Milan Linate/Rome Fiumicino bases, competitive overcapacity in beach markets, and an unexpected £25m fuel-price/£32m legal-provision hit; easyJet holidays PBT up 39% to £61m; net cash of £434m and £4.7bn total liquidity
Kenton Jarvis (former CFO) formally took over as CEO from Johan Lundgren (who stepped down in early 2025 after seven years); Jan De Raeymaeker joined as new CFO

FY2025 annual results: record revenue £10.1bn (+9%), headline PBT £665m (+9%), easyJet holidays PBT £250m (+32%) hitting its medium-term target two years early (now upgraded to £450m by FY30); net cash improved to £602m; dividend raised 9% to 13.2p/share

guidance.as_of: Q3 FY2026 Trading Update (23 July 2026) and H1 FY2026 Results Presentation (21 May 2026)

items.notes: ASK capacity expected to grow c.6% YoY as sector lengths increase; H1 was +4% seats/+8% ASKs, H2 moderating to +2% seats/+5% ASKs
From a base of 3.1m FY25 customers; holidays 87% sold for Q4 FY26 as of July 2026 update, taking market share in a competitive environment
Unchanged long-standing target; FY2025 headline PBT was £665m, so material improvement still required
Upgraded from prior £250m target after that target was achieved two years early in FY2025 (£250m actual)
FY2025 achieved 18.0% headline ROCE (vs 16.1% FY2024); management notes this target becomes 'more demanding' as capital employed grows with new aircraft deliveries
FY2025 headline PBT per seat was £6.39 (+£0.31 YoY)

items.target: c.£250 million incremental annual cost efficiencies
items.notes: Driven by accelerated A319 retirement (all A319s retired by FY29) and larger-gauge A320neo/A321neo deliveries (17 in FY26, 30 in FY27, 43 in FY28)

items.target: increase by low single digits YoY
items.notes: Consistent with Q3 CASK ex-fuel performance of +3% YoY
Booked position improved 1ppt YoY vs the half-year update in May; every 1ppt move in Q4 RASK is ~£33m of revenue; every $100/MT fuel move is ~£17m cost impact (79% hedged at $786/MT for Q4)
From £5.0bn as at H1 FY2026, reflecting continued fleet ownership growth

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Kenton Jarvis described Q3 FY26 as impacted by the Middle East conflict's effect on fuel prices and consumer booking trends, but noted strong late-booking demand, improving operational performance (YTD OTP 78%, +2ppts) and rising customer satisfaction. Management reiterated focus on 'self-help' initiatives — upgauging, digitalisation, and easyJet holidays scaling — to drive medium-term margin and profit improvement 'as conditions normalise', while flagging that H1 FY27 capacity growth will moderate after three years of elevated asset-utilisation-driven growth. Separately, the FY2025 Chair's statement emphasized that the pending Apollo transaction (announced after FY25 year-end) is a distinct corporate event from ongoing operational guidance.

bull_case: Apollo Global's agreed £7.15/share all-cash offer provides a firm, largely de-risked floor for shareholders (subject to completion risk), with the stock likely to trade close to the offer price as the deal approaches its targeted Q1 2027 close

easyJet holidays is a high-growth, high-margin, capital-light business that has already beaten its medium-term profit target two years early and has a credible, upgraded £450m FY30 PBT target with low execution risk given its asset-light model

Fleet upgauging (A319 retirement, NEO deliveries) is a clear, quantified cost-efficiency lever (~£250m/year by FY28) layered on top of revenue growth, supporting margin expansion independent of ticket pricing

Strong balance sheet (net cash £602m at FY25 year-end, £4.7bn total liquidity, investment-grade credit rating) gives resilience to fund growth and absorb fuel/geopolitical shocks without diluting shareholders
Leading slot positions at primary European airports represent a durable, hard-to-replicate competitive asset relative to secondary-airport competitors
bear_case: Deal completion risk is now the dominant driver of the share price: EU/UK airline-ownership rules have already delayed the Scheme Document once (to 15 October 2026), and any failure to satisfy regulators, win 75% shareholder approval, or secure financing could see the stock reprice sharply below the offer level

Underlying airline economics remain structurally challenged versus Ryanair's lower cost base, with persistent winter losses, competitive overcapacity in beach markets, and RASK declines (airline RASK -3% in FY2025, further pressure in H1 FY26) showing the medium-term >£1bn PBT target is not yet close

Geopolitical and fuel-price shocks (Middle East conflict driving fuel to ~$1,800/MT in April 2026) can swing quarterly profits dramatically, as shown by the Q3 FY26 PBT collapse to £85m from £286m a year earlier

Regulatory and compliance costs are rising structurally (ETS free-allowance phase-out from FY26, diverging UK/EU SAF mandates, EU261 disruption compensation), compressing margins independent of commercial execution

Capital intensity remains high (owned asset base targeted to exceed £7.5bn by FY28), and continued fleet growth could pressure the net cash position if demand softens or deliveries accelerate faster than cash generation
